result.summary: Iolaus encourages Heracles before the fight with Cycnus and Ares, and Heracles answers, then arms himself with the gifts of the gods. The long description of his glittering shield begins, with its images of Fear, Strife, snakes, beasts, the battle of Lapiths and Centaurs, Ares, Athene and the gods on Olympus.

scenes.title: Iolaus encourages Heracles
scenes.summary: Iolaus says Zeus and Poseidon favour Heracles and urges him to arm. Heracles, pleased, tells Iolaus to handle the horse Arion well.
scenes.stakes: Heracles faces a hard battle against a strong foe and the war god.

scenes.title: Heracles puts on his armour
scenes.summary: Heracles dons greaves from Hephaestus, a breast-plate from Athene, a quiver of arrows, spear and adamant helm.
scenes.stakes: His life in the coming fight.

scenes.title: The shield: Fear and Strife
scenes.summary: The unbreakable shield shows Fear, Strife, Fate and twelve snake heads that terrify his enemies.

scenes.title: Beasts, Lapiths and Ares
scenes.summary: The shield also shows boars and lions, the Lapiths fighting the Centaurs, and Ares in his chariot.

scenes.title: Athene and the gods on Olympus
scenes.summary: Athene goes toward the strife, and Apollo plays his lyre among the gods on Olympus while the Muses sing.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Poseidon; text does not name him here.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid image of Fear on the shield, opening the famous ekphrasis.

analysis.text: Arming scenes build heroic stature; the shield's terrors show Heracles as bringer of death, backed by the gods.
The shield imitates the Homeric shield of Achilles, a literary ekphrasis of an imagined divine object.

legacy.text: The shield description belongs to the ekphrasis tradition that includes Achilles' shield in the Iliad and Aeneas' in the Aeneid.

fun_facts.text: The Shield of Heracles was attributed to Hesiod in antiquity, though many scholars doubt he wrote it.

language_notes.text: "Earth-Shaker" is a standard epithet of Poseidon, god of the sea and earthquakes; "veil of walls" is a poetic phrase for Thebe's encircling walls.
"Son of Iphiclus" is Iolaus himself; "Alcides" is Heracles, named for his grandfather Alcaeus. The "two sons" are thus Heracles and his nephew Iolaus.
"Winged words" is a Homeric formula for words that fly swiftly from speaker to hearer.
"The steel that saves men from doom" is an obscure periphrasis, probably meaning a sword slung over his shoulder.
"In front they had death" means the arrowheads were poisoned; "trickled with tears" refers to the dripping venom.
"Adamant" denotes an unbreakably hard metal, not a known real one.
"Electrum" is a pale alloy of gold and silver; "cyanus" is a dark blue substance, perhaps enamel or glass paste. The "1802" is a stray footnote marker.
"Parching Sirius" is the Dog Star, whose rising marks the hottest season of summer.
"Scion" means offspring or descendant; Mopsus is described as a descendant of Ares.
A diviner is a seer who foretells events by omens; Asbolus was known for this among the Centaurs.
Fear and Flight are personified powers (Phobos and Deimos in Greek tradition) that attend Ares in battle.
Tritogeneia is an epithet of Athene, of uncertain meaning. The text is garbled at the end: "spoil 1803" is a printing error, probably for "spoil" (driver of the spoil).
"Son of Zeus and Leto" is Apollo, whose instrument is the lyre.

context_notes.text: The "car of Ares" belongs to Cycnus, son of Ares, whom Heracles is about to fight in his chariot.
Arion is Heracles' legendary swift horse; Iolaus, his nephew, serves as his charioteer.
Hephaestus was the smith god who made armour and tools for gods and heroes.
Athene (Pallas) was Heracles' patron and helped him through his labours.
The Lapiths fought the Centaurs after the Centaurs misbehaved at Peirithous' wedding feast; it was a favourite subject in Greek art.
The aegis was Athene's protective goatskin cloak or breastplate, a symbol of divine power and terror.
The Muses were goddesses of song and the arts; Pieria, near Olympus, was their traditional home.

literary_notes.text: Fear is shown as a figure with glowing eyes, turning an abstract emotion into a terrifying image.
Strife acts as a pitiless being who steals minds, making war itself a character.
Fate holding wounded, unwounded and dead men gives a grim, vivid picture of war's range of outcomes.
Snakes that clash their teeth and frighten all of Heracles' foes exaggerate the shield's magical power.
Vivid detail of dark blood dripping and outstretched necks makes the carved scene feel like real death.
The golden figures move "as though they were alive," praising the craftsmanship of the shield.
Ares is shown red with blood, as if slaying real men, defining him as a god of savage war.
Apollo's sweet music among the gods offsets the violent battle scenes before it, showing peace beside war on the shield.
